records.sourceFile: Location of hamstring injuries based on magnetic resonance imaging - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Grange S, Reurink G, Nguyen AQ, Riviera-Navarro C, Foschia C, Croisille P, et al. Location of Hamstring Injuries Based on Magnetic Resonance Imaging: A Systematic Review. Sports Health. 2022.
paper.abstract: From 2788 records in five databases, the authors included 34 MRI studies of 2761 acute hamstring injuries. The long head of the biceps femoris was most often affected (70%) and the myotendinous junction was the most common tissue (52%). The abstract describes the proximal, central and distal distribution as homogeneous and notes that MRI reports of hamstring injuries are often poor.
paper.tldr: Across 34 MRI studies of 2761 acute hamstring injuries, the long head of the biceps femoris and the myotendinous junction were most often involved. Reporting of injury location was inconsistent, so the even proximal-central-distal split should not be assumed to apply to every squad.
paper.methods: The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42018107580) and searched PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library on March 1, 2020. Included studies reported MRI-based location of acute indirect hamstring injuries performed within 8 days of injury, and case reports and reviews were excluded. Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts, one reviewer rated risk of bias with a 14-item checklist (75% cut-off), and the data were summarized descriptively.
paper.findings: Of 34 studies, 26 were prospective and 8 retrospective, with 97.4% of injured participants men and 83.3% high-level athletes. The long head of the biceps femoris was involved in 69.8% of 1068 injuries (20 studies) and was the primary lesion in 76.9% of 2438 injuries (30 studies) in the text, and the myotendinous junction was the most common tissue (51.9% of 1286 injuries, 18 studies). Proximal, central and distal shares were 34.0%, 33.4% and 32.6% in 8 studies (344 injuries), while 7 other studies (713 injuries) reporting only proximal versus distal found lesions mostly proximal (62.8%). Sprinting accounted for 55.3% and stretching for 3.0% of 788 injuries with a reported mechanism (9 studies); of the 24 stretching injuries, 14 involved the semimembranosus and 13 its proximal tendon.
paper.limitations: The abstract presents the even proximal-central-distal split as describing 'all lesions', but it rests on 8 studies with 344 injuries; 7 other studies with 713 injuries found mostly proximal lesions, and the body's own conclusion calls the location distribution 'inhomogeneous'. The abstract's claim that the stretching mechanism leads to a longer time out from sport is not supported by any time-loss data in the text, and the primary-lesion share for the long head of the biceps femoris is 76.9% in the text but 79.6% in Table 2. Table 1 notes that some studies may involve identical or overlapping populations that were included separately, and only 2 studies described tissue within each muscle head, English-language studies only were included, and a single reviewer rated risk of bias.
paper.practicalImplications: Recording muscle head, tissue and location on early MRI, as the authors advise, can make a hamstring injury more specific for staff reporting and rehabilitation planning. The most common pattern (long head of the biceps femoris, myotendinous junction) is a useful starting point, but no single injury classification is agreed, so staff should state the classification they use.
paper.athleteDev: Sprinting accounted for 55.3% of acute hamstring injuries where mechanism was reported (9 studies, 788 injuries), which points to high-speed running as the main context in these sports. The review is descriptive and does not test training changes, so it cannot show which sprint or conditioning loads reduce injury.
paper.rtp: The review describes where injuries sit on early MRI, which can help classify a hamstring injury, but it does not report time to return to play or recurrence rates. It should not be used to set return-to-sport timing.

records.sourceFile: London International Consensus and Delphi study on hamstring injuries Part 1 - Classification.pdf

paper.citation: Paton BM, Court N, Giakoumis M, Head P, Kayani B, Kelly S, et al. London International Consensus and Delphi study on hamstring injuries part 1: classification. Br J Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: This modified Delphi study combined a narrative evidence review with expert surveys and a consensus meeting on how to classify hamstring injuries. Experts agreed that MRI is the preferred imaging, that classification should use one agreed terminology, and that systems should separate individual hamstring muscles and include mechanism and functional criteria. The authors note that no current classification predicts time to return to sport or reinjury.
paper.tldr: An international expert panel agreed that MRI is the preferred imaging for hamstring injuries and that one agreed terminology is needed, with the BAMIC system the most used. The authors state that current classifications do not predict return to sport or reinjury, so they should be used to describe injury anatomy rather than set timelines.
paper.methods: This was a modified Delphi study with a narrative evidence review. Round 1 was a digital survey of 46 invited experts (35 responded), followed by a two-day face-to-face consensus meeting with 15 experts and a round 2 survey of 99 respondents (of 112 invited) voting on 18 statements. Statements were accepted at 70% or more agreement, and athletes were not included as participants.
paper.findings: In the round 2 survey, MRI was judged the preferred imaging for diagnosis and classification (89.5%), agreed terminology was supported (91.8%), and one main classification system was supported (84.8%). Imaging was judged vital for classification (70.5%), but the statement that anatomical classification is essential for diagnosis reached only 62.0%, and the statements on surgical criteria (52.1%) and a registry (68.7%) did not reach the 70% threshold. The BAMIC system was the most used (56 of 96 votes, 58%), ahead of Munich and Barcelona.
paper.limitations: Only 15 of 35 first-round respondents attended the meeting, women were few (18 of 99 in the final survey; Table 2 gives 2 of 35 in round 1 although the text says 2 of 39), and experts from Asia, Africa and South America were under-represented; athletes were not included. Several agreement levels in the discussion differ from Table 7, which is reported here: anatomical, radiological parameters 95.1% in text vs 95.9% in Table 7, free vs central tendon 86.1% vs 86.9%, surgical criteria 51.2% vs 52.1%, ultrasound as primary imaging after 48 hours 21.8% vs 25.8%, and BAMIC use 57% vs 58% in Table 3; the text also cites 70.3% and 56.6% for imaging being essential for classification and diagnosis, against 70.5% and 62.0% for the closest Table 7 statements. Respondents chose which survey domains to answer, and most classification systems lack validity or reliability data.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should record the affected muscle, tissue, location and mechanism of a hamstring injury in one agreed terminology, as the panel recommends. Clinical signs such as bruising, loss of muscle tension, palpable defect or significant weakness should prompt imaging, and the panel's recommended MRI timing is 24 to 48 hours after injury. Functional criteria and patient-reported outcome measures should be used alongside any classification.
paper.athleteDev: The consensus supports consistent recording of injury site, tissue and mechanism so that staff can compare injuries across a squad and season. It does not provide training load thresholds or performance targets.
paper.rtp: The panel recommends that functional criteria and patient-reported outcomes run alongside classification in rehabilitation decisions. The authors state that no current classification predicts time to return to sport or reinjury, so the classification should not be used to set return-to-sport timing.

records.sourceFile: London International Consensus and Delphi study on hamstring injuries Part 2 - Operative management.pdf

paper.citation: Plastow R, Kerkhoffs GMMJ, Wood D, Paton BM, Kayani B, Pollock N, et al. London International Consensus and Delphi study on hamstring injuries part 2: operative management. Br J Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: A literature review and modified Delphi process were used to produce consensus statements on operative management of hamstring injuries. Experts agreed on surgical indications for proximal avulsions with gapping or loss of tension, symptomatic displaced bony avulsions and proximal free tendon injuries with functional compromise, and agreed that corticosteroid injections have no role for undisplaced avulsions. Agreement was not reached on surgery reducing recurrence or on endoscopic fixation.
paper.tldr: An international expert panel agreed on several indications for surgery on hamstring injuries, mainly high-grade proximal avulsions with gapping or loss of tension, and agreed that corticosteroid injections should not be used for undisplaced avulsions. Agreement was not reached that surgery reduces reinjury, and the authors describe that benefit as unproven.
paper.methods: This was a modified Delphi study built on a literature search of PubMed, CINAHL, Cochrane and EMBASE up to January 2020, which identified 1626 articles and used 146 after screening, with no quality appraisal tool. Round 1 surveyed 46 invited experts (35 responded), a consensus meeting drafted statements, and a round 2 online survey of 99 respondents (of 112 invited) voted true, false or undecided, with 70% agreement as the threshold. Athletes were not included as survey participants.
paper.findings: Round 2 statements reaching 70% agreement (Table 1) included surgery for gapping at the zone of tendinous injury (87.2%), loss of muscle tension (70.7%), loss of muscle and tendon tension producing a gap in proximal free tendon injuries (83.5%), risk of functional loss or performance deficit with non-operative management (72.2%) and symptomatic displaced bony avulsions of the ischium (72.8%), plus indications depending on anatomy, athlete demands and expected outcome (87.1%) and surgery's capacity to restore anatomy and function (87.1%). Corticosteroid injections for undisplaced avulsions were agreed to have no role (80%). Agreement was not reached that surgery reduces recurrence (48.2% overall, 70% among surgeons), speeds recovery (36.0%), that fixation should be endoscopic (9.5% in Table 1) or that avulsed ischial bone should be resected (31.2% in Table 1).
paper.limitations: Counts conflict within the paper: the text reports 15 of 35 round 1 respondents at the meeting and women as 2 of 39, while Table 2 lists 38 round 1 respondents and 14 meeting members but sex splits summing to 35 and 15; the discussion gives 9.8% and 29.3% agreement for endoscopic fixation and bone resection where Table 1 gives 9.5% and 31.2%, and it says six statements were agreed although Table 1 shows eight above 70%. The evidence base is small uncontrolled case series and expert opinion, the literature search used no quality appraisal, and non-surgeons were allowed to vote on surgical statements. The panel had few women, no athletes and limited representation from Asia, Africa and South America.
paper.practicalImplications: For complete proximal avulsions with gapping or loss of tension, surgery should be considered and weighed against the athlete's sporting demands and expected function, with early repair preferred once surgery is chosen. Corticosteroid injections should not be used for undisplaced avulsions, and endoscopic fixation or a claimed reduction in reinjury should be treated as unproven. Lower-demand patients whose daily function is not significantly affected may consider non-operative care.
paper.athleteDev: The authors state that high-demand athletes cannot accept decrements in strength or performance, so surgery for a high-grade proximal avulsion should be discussed early in those athletes. The consensus gives no training load, sprint or performance targets.
paper.rtp: The authors cite uncontrolled case series reporting return to pre-injury sporting level after surgical repair in high-level athletes, but the panel did not establish return-to-sport timelines or reinjury rates after surgery. The paper should not be used to set return-to-sport timing for operative or non-operative care.

records.sourceFile: Lower knee flexion and hip extension rate of torque development in athletes with previous hamstring strain injury.pdf

paper.citation: Buhmann R, Trajano GS, Kerr GK, Shield AJ. Lower knee flexion and hip extension rate of torque development in athletes with previous hamstring strain injury. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2021.
paper.abstract: In 10 male athletes with a previous unilateral hamstring strain and 10 without, previously injured limbs had slower rate of torque development (-31%, p = 0.02) and slower biceps femoris sEMG rise (p = 0.003) during intended eccentric knee flexion than control limbs. Both injured and uninjured limbs had slower hip extensor rate of torque development than control limbs. The authors suggest these findings may reflect lower descending input to hamstring motoneurons in previously injured athletes.
paper.tldr: Ten male athletes with a past hamstring strain had slower rate of torque development and biceps femoris EMG rise during intended eccentric knee flexion than controls, and both legs were slower in hip extension. The retrospective design cannot show whether these deficits cause or result from injury.
paper.methods: Retrospective comparison of 20 recreationally active males who played soccer, sprinting, rugby league or rugby union. Ten had a unilateral hamstring strain 3 to 24 months earlier (all biceps femoris long head, self-reported grade 2), and ten had no history. Participants completed two familiarisation sessions, then isokinetic dynamometry with intended isometric, concentric and eccentric knee flexion (order randomised) and isometric hip extension, with surface EMG on the biceps femoris and medial hamstrings. Control limbs were averaged across dominant and non-dominant limbs. Rate of torque development and sEMG rise were calculated over 50 and 100 ms and analysed with two-way ANOVA (limb by time) and Bonferroni post hoc tests.
paper.findings: During intended eccentric knee flexion, rate of torque development was lower in previously injured limbs than in control limbs (-204 Nm/s, -31%, 95% CI -377 to -32, p = 0.02, d = 0.62) and uninjured limbs (-187 Nm/s, -29%, p = 0.03, d = 0.59). Biceps femoris sEMG rise was lower in injured limbs than in controls (-181% per second, 95% CI -308 to -54, p = 0.003, d = 1.10). During isometric hip extension, rate of torque development was lower in injured limbs (-323 Nm/s, -29%, p = 0.01, d = 0.85) and in uninjured limbs (-337 Nm/s, -31%, p = 0.007, d = 0.73) than in controls. Concentric and isometric knee flexion showed no limb difference, and time since injury was unrelated to any outcome.
paper.limitations: Ten men per group, a retrospective design, and self-reported injury grade, so causation cannot be established. The 'eccentric' contractions were largely isometric for the first 100 to 150 ms before the dynamometer lever moved, and the authors note that surface EMG cannot establish voluntary activation. The analysis is described as a two-way ANOVA with no stated handling of each injured participant contributing two limbs. The authors could not separate hamstring from other hip extensors such as adductor magnus or gluteus maximus. Within-participant coefficients of variation for rate of torque development were 8 to 15%.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could consider measuring rate of torque development in both limbs during rapid knee flexion and hip extension when assessing athletes after hamstring injury, since this study found about 30% differences between previously injured and control limbs. The uninjured limb was also slower than controls in hip extension, so a limb-symmetry comparison could miss this deficit. The study does not test whether training changes these measures or whether they predict re-injury, so they should not be used as a clearance threshold on their own.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Explosive torque production and biceps femoris activation were lower in previously injured limbs, which may matter for sprinting and deceleration. The study did not measure sprint or sport performance, so the link to performance is inferred.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Deficits in rate of torque development and EMG were still present 3 to 24 months after strain injury, which suggests they may persist after rehabilitation. The design cannot show whether they cause or result from injury, and no return-to-sport outcomes were recorded, so the findings cannot set a clearance criterion.

records.sourceFile: M. biceps femoris – A wolf in sheep’s clothing- The downside of a lower limb injury prevention training.pdf

paper.citation: Ertelt T, Gronwald T. M. biceps femoris - A wolf in sheep’s clothing: The downside of a lower limb injury prevention training. Med Hypotheses. 2017;109:119-125.
paper.abstract: This hypothesis article proposes that lower limb injury prevention training may change biceps femoris activation patterns and insertion-dependent knee mechanics, which could raise hamstring injury susceptibility. The proposal is supported by a single simulated one-legged stopping maneuver in an 80 kg model.
paper.tldr: A simulated stopping maneuver suggests that biceps femoris insertion site and activation level change knee mechanics, which could in theory affect hamstring injury risk after prevention training. The idea has not been tested in athletes.
paper.methods: The authors built a simplified muscle-driven forward dynamics model of an 80 kg male performing a one-legged stopping maneuver after running at 2 m/s, using MATLAB/SimMechanics. Biceps femoris was set to a tibial or fibular insertion configuration and activated at 0%, 50% or 100%, and knee extension or flexion was compared across these conditions.
paper.findings: With biceps femoris activated at 100% and a tibial insertion, the model showed noticeable knee extension during the stop, whereas with a distal fibular insertion it showed noticeable knee flexion over the same time frame. At 0% activation, knee extension was produced by rectus femoris and vastus intermedius. The authors describe the effect of a minor increase in activation as large for the tibial insertion, based on a lever ratio of about 4:1 in one case and 2:1 in the other. No statistical analysis is reported.
paper.limitations: The results come from one simulated subject and a simplified six-muscle model, with no experimental, EMG, MRI or athlete data. The authors acknowledge that the findings must be verified in a controlled experimental setting. The hypothesis that training increases injury risk is not tested, and the paper contains no statistical analysis.
paper.practicalImplications: The paper does not support changing current hamstring prevention programmes. It proposes that insertion geometry and individual activation patterns could be assessed in future studies, and that these might inform individualised programmes. Staff should treat this as a hypothesis for research, not a basis for changing athlete programmes.
paper.athleteDev: This paper cannot guide athlete training prescription. It suggests that individual differences in biceps femoris activation could in theory affect knee mechanics, which is a question to test rather than a basis for changing programmes.
paper.rtp: This paper cannot inform return to sport decisions. It includes no injured athletes and no return-to-play outcomes; the only re-injury figures are background citations from other studies.

records.sourceFile: MMP3 single‐nucleotide polymorphisms are associated with noncontact ACL injuries in competing high level athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Simunic-Briski N, Vrgoc G, Knjaz D, Jankovic S, Dembic Z, Lauc G. MMP3 single-nucleotide polymorphisms are associated with noncontact ACL injuries in competing high-level athletes. J Orthop Res. 2024;42:109-114.
paper.abstract: This case-control genetic association study compared Croatian athletes with noncontact ACL rupture against retired professional athletes without ACL injury. Three MMP3 single-nucleotide polymorphisms were associated with ACL rupture status, with the rs591058 TT, rs650108 GG and rs679620 AA genotypes and the T-G-A haplotype over-represented in the ACL group.
paper.tldr: In a small Croatian case-control study, three MMP3 genotypes and one haplotype were more common in athletes with noncontact ACL rupture than in retired athletes without ACL injury. The association is unreplicated and the reported odds ratios need checking.
paper.methods: A case-control study recruited 95 athletes with MRI and arthroscopically confirmed noncontact ACL rupture (2016-2017) and 92 retired professional athletes with no ACL injury during their careers. Three MMP3 SNPs (rs591058, rs650108, rs679620) were genotyped by pyrosequencing, and allele, genotype and haplotype frequencies were compared using odds ratios, with Hardy-Weinberg and linkage analyses and false discovery rate adjustment. No power analysis was performed.
paper.findings: Genotype frequencies differed for all three SNPs: TT for rs591058 was 29.4% (28/95) in cases and 9.8% (9/92) in controls (p = 0.0012); GG for rs650108 was 54.7% (52/95) vs 33.7% (31/92) (p = 0.0051); and AA for rs679620 was 27.4% (26/95) vs 9.8% (9/92) (p = 0.0030). The T-G-A haplotype was more frequent in cases (97 vs 68 haplotypes, p = 0.0104, OR 1.71, 95% CI 1.13-2.59) and C-A-G was more frequent in controls (OR 0.55). The printed genotype odds ratios (38.541, 23.338 and 34.750) lie outside their printed 95% CIs (1.7024-8.7254, 1.2899-4.2226 and 1.5266-7.9101), and the text does not resolve which value is correct.
paper.limitations: The sample is small, controls were older (39.0 vs 25.8 years) and heavier and were not matched on age or weight, and no replication cohort was used. The text has internal number conflicts: genotype odds ratios lie outside their own confidence intervals, rs591058 allele frequencies print as 48.9% and 52.1% (summing to 101%), and haplotype counts in Table 3 sum to 182 controls and 192 cases rather than 184 and 190. The abstract describes professional athletes while the methods describe recreationally competing or professional athletes, and injury mechanism was self-reported.
paper.practicalImplications: The study does not support using MMP3 genotype to screen, select or rank athletes for ACL risk, because no screening tool was tested and the association is unreplicated. Current practice should not change on the basis of this paper. The authors' suggestion of future screening is a research question.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not inform athlete training or performance programming. Staff should not use these genotypes to classify athletes' ACL risk or to guide training decisions.
paper.rtp: This study compares athletes with ACL rupture to controls and reports no return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Mapping of the Pharmacological Effect of Prohibited Substances and Methods to Athletic Physiological Characteristics.pdf

paper.citation: Hayward G, Gaborini L, Robinson N, Stuart M, Mottram D. Mapping of the Pharmacological Effect of Prohibited Substances and Methods to Athletic Physiological Characteristics. Drug Testing and Analysis. 2025.
paper.abstract: The authors built a physio-pharmacological scoring framework that maps the expected performance effects of WADA Prohibited List categories onto the physiological demands of 160 Olympic disciplines. They propose that the framework can inform anti-doping risk assessment and test distribution planning.
paper.tldr: Expert ratings estimate which prohibited substances and methods could most help each Olympic discipline, based on its physiological demands. The authors propose using these estimates to plan anti-doping testing, though the ratings are theoretical and expert agreement was low.
paper.methods: Eight experts rated 31 pharmacological categories on six athletic demands using a 5-point scale, and a gene and cell doping category was excluded because of disagreement. Ratings were aggregated by majority vote, mapped to each discipline's demands with a calibrated scoring function and bilinear interpolation, and reliability was assessed with Krippendorff's alpha.
paper.findings: Krippendorff's alpha was 0.55 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.61), which the authors describe as low agreement. The mapping gives strong potential advantages to anabolic agents for strength and power disciplines and to erythropoietin and blood manipulation for aerobic endurance, while narcotics and cannabinoids show negative effects. Diuretics show limited direct performance effects, which the authors attribute to their masking role.
paper.limitations: The scores are not compared with International Federation testing or sample data, so the authors cannot show that high-scoring substances are the ones detected. The authors also note that non-performance motives for doping are outside the scope of the study.
paper.practicalImplications: Anti-doping test planning could weight testing toward substances with high estimated benefit for a discipline's physiological demands, as the authors propose. Staff should treat the scores as a hypothesis for risk planning, not as evidence of use by any athlete.
paper.athleteDev: The paper links physiological demands to theoretical performance effects by discipline, which helps explain anti-doping risk. It gives no training or performance guidance, and it should not be used to judge an athlete's performance.
paper.rtp: The paper does not address rehabilitation or return to sport. It covers performance effects only, and it does not assess health harms of the listed substances.

records.sourceFile: Mechanisms of acute ankle syndesmosis ligament injuries in professional male rugby union players - A systematic visual video analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Delahunt E, Farrell G, Boylan A, Kerin F, Tierney P, Hogan H, et al. Mechanisms of acute ankle syndesmosis ligament injuries in professional male rugby union players: a systematic visual video analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2020.
paper.abstract: The authors used retrospective video analysis to describe how acute ankle syndesmosis ligament injuries occurred in male professional rugby union players at one club. Three physiotherapists independently assessed the videos, reached a consensus, and described each injury mechanism.
paper.tldr: Most of the 13 included syndesmosis injuries happened while players were being tackled or were tackling. The study describes a common limb position at injury, but it is small and comes from one club.
paper.methods: Retrospective review of 30 time-loss syndesmosis injuries from one professional club's surveillance database, with video available for 27 and the mechanism visible in 13. Three physiotherapists assessed the videos independently, reached consensus, and wrote a qualitative description of each mechanism.
paper.findings: Six injuries (46%) were direct contact and seven (54%) indirect contact injuries, with seven sustained while being tackled and six while tackling. The anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament was injured in all 13 cases, and the most common limb position was hip and knee flexion, knee valgus, ankle dorsiflexion, pronation and external rotation of the foot. The authors judged tackle mechanics suboptimal in all six tackling injuries, and ten cases were managed surgically with a mean time to unrestricted training of 61 days (SD 25).
paper.limitations: Only 13 injuries from one club were analysed, because the injury event was not visible in 14 of the 27 videos. The moment of injury was estimated by subjective consensus, and video quality, resolution and camera angle limited the analysis. The paper's counts are internally inconsistent: it reports 6 direct and 7 indirect contact injuries, but the case descriptions classify 5 as direct and 8 as indirect (case #9 is labelled both), and it reports 8 right and 7 left ankles for 13 injuries while Tables 1 and 2 list 8 right and 5 left.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians assessing a rugby player with an ankle injury should consider a syndesmosis injury when the history includes external rotation of the foot, forced pronation or forced dorsiflexion. Coaches can use the tackle examples to review footwork and tackle technique, but the study cannot show how often each mechanism causes injury.
paper.athleteDev: Use the described tackling situations to review tackle technique and footwork with professional players, recognising that the evidence is descriptive and comes from a small sample.
paper.rtp: The study reports a mean time to unrestricted training of 61 days for these 13 cases, but it sets no return-to-play criteria and tests no readiness measures, so it should not be used to decide when a player can return to play.

records.sourceFile: Mechanisms of hamstring strain injury - Interactions between fatigue, muscle activation and function.pdf

paper.citation: Huygaerts S, Cos F, Cohen DD, Calleja-González J, Guitart M, Blazevich AJ, et al. Mechanisms of hamstring strain injury: interactions between fatigue, muscle activation and function. Sports. 2020;8:65.
paper.abstract: The authors review evidence on sprint-type hamstring strain injury mechanisms, focusing on the late swing and early stance phases of running. They also discuss how neuromuscular fatigue may change hamstring activation, coordination and function, and how this could relate to injury risk.
paper.tldr: Hamstring injury mechanisms during sprinting are still unclear, and most mechanical evidence comes from non-fatigued athletes. Fatigue may alter muscle coordination and running mechanics in ways that could raise strain risk, but this link has not been tested in injury data.
paper.methods: Narrative critical review with no search method reported. The authors summarise biomechanical modelling, EMG and fatigue studies, and tabulate 13 modelling or EMG studies that measured non-fatigued participants, plus two case reports.
paper.findings: The authors conclude that the late swing and early stance phases are the points at which sprint-type injury is most likely, while stating that the evidence on which phase carries the greatest risk is inconclusive. They propose fatigue-related changes that could raise strain risk, including altered hamstring coordination, earlier fatigue of biceps femoris and rectus femoris than of other lower limb muscles during high-speed running, reduced horizontal force after repeated sprints, increased anterior pelvic tilt, and reduced lower limb stiffness with a 'Groucho' running pattern. These links are drawn from separate studies and have not been tested as injury predictors.
paper.limitations: No search or appraisal method is described, and the review does not grade the strength of the evidence it cites. Most mechanical evidence comes from simulation models and small samples of non-fatigued athletes, and the authors note that these models omit tissue complexity and fatigue effects.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not treat the late swing and early stance phases as established injury windows, because the authors describe the evidence as inconclusive. Fatigue monitoring during high-speed running work can be framed as a hypothesis to test, since the review gives no thresholds or validated tests for practice. Hamstring and synergist strength-endurance work is presented as an area for further study rather than a proven intervention.
paper.athleteDev: Use the review to frame questions about how fatigue changes sprint mechanics and hamstring coordination, not as a basis for fatigue thresholds or sprint prescriptions. Check any speed or fatigue monitoring against each player's own baseline.
paper.rtp: The review addresses mechanisms of hamstring strain during sprinting. It does not evaluate rehabilitation, return-to-sport testing or re-injury criteria, so it should not be used to set return-to-running or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Medical disqualification following concussion in collegiate student-athletes - Findings from the CARE Consortium.pdf

paper.citation: Schmidt JD, Weber Rawlins ML, Lynall RC, D'Lauro C, Clugston JR, McAllister TW, et al. Medical disqualification following concussion in collegiate student-athletes: findings from the CARE Consortium. Sports Med. 2020.
paper.abstract: The authors compared premorbid and postmorbid factors between NCAA student-athletes who were and were not medically disqualified after concussion, using CARE Consortium data. Disqualification was uncommon and was associated with prior concussions, headaches, a more immediate initial presentation and a longer, more complicated recovery.
paper.tldr: Medical disqualification after concussion was uncommon (2.9%) in this collegiate sample. Disqualified athletes more often had prior concussions, recent headaches, immediate removal from play and longer, more complicated recoveries, but the study is exploratory and cannot set a disqualification rule.
paper.methods: Prospectively collected CARE Consortium data from 1,832 NCAA varsity student-athletes diagnosed with concussion across 29 sites, using each athlete's most recent concussion. Baseline and serial symptom, cognitive and balance assessments, and clinician case report forms were compared between 53 medically disqualified and 1,779 non-disqualified athletes with chi-square, Fisher's exact, ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests, and unadjusted odds ratios were calculated for factors that were significant or trending.
paper.findings: Two prior concussions (OR 3.2) and three or more (OR 7.4) were associated with disqualification, as were one or more headaches in the past three months (OR 1.8) and immediate removal from play (OR 2.4), while delayed symptom onset was linked to lower odds (OR 0.43). Clinician-reported prolonged recovery due to mental health alterations (OR 5.3), motivation or malingering (OR 7.5) or other injuries (OR 3.7) was also associated, as were alcohol (OR 2.6), tobacco (OR 3.3) and marijuana (OR 5.4) use since injury, and disqualified athletes took longer to become asymptomatic (23.5 vs 10.6 days, p < 0.001). Sex, sport, division, loss of consciousness and amnesia did not differ, and some athletes were disqualified with few prior concussions while others with three or more were not.
paper.limitations: The authors describe the study as exploratory. Only 53 athletes were disqualified, the odds ratios are unadjusted with wide confidence intervals, and several recovery factors reflect the clinician's impression. Disqualification included season-only decisions, formal disqualification may miss athletes whose eligibility ended, and site practices were not recorded. The results text assigns the substance-use odds ratios to different substances than the abstract (the abstract matches Table 5 counts), and the discussion says 32.1% of disqualified athletes had one prior concussion while Table 3 gives 32.1% with none.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff managing collegiate concussion should record prior concussion and recent headache history, because these were the only premorbid factors that differed. A prolonged recovery with mental health alterations, substance use or apparent motivation problems should prompt closer clinical management, and the authors suggest exploring treatments such as cognitive behavioural therapy before a final disqualification decision. The authors state that no set number of concussions should force disqualification and that immediate removal should not be treated as predictive, so these factors should inform rather than determine the decision.
paper.athleteDev: This study describes clinical disqualification decisions and has little direct performance application. It can support conversations with athletes about why concussion history and recovery course feature in eligibility decisions, without implying a fixed concussion limit.
paper.rtp: The study describes who was medically disqualified after concussion, not who can safely return. It sets no return criteria and should not be used to decide whether an individual athlete is cleared or disqualified after concussion.

records.sourceFile: Modeling Training Loads and Injuries- The Dangers of Discretization.pdf

paper.citation: Carey DL, Crossley KM, Whiteley R, Mosler A, Ong KL, Crow J, et al. Modeling training loads and injuries: the dangers of discretization. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2018;50(11):2267-2276.
paper.abstract: This simulation study compared discrete and continuous models of the relationship between workload (ACWR) and injury risk, using workload data from an Australian football club and a soccer league. Injuries were simulated from three predefined risk profiles. Discrete models produced more false discoveries (16% to 21%) than continuous models (3% to 7%), and AUC selected a discrete model in more than 30% of simulations, while Brier and logarithmic scores selected discrete models in 6% or fewer.
paper.tldr: Splitting a continuous training load variable such as ACWR into categories gave poorer injury risk models than spline or fractional polynomial methods in simulated data. Calibration measures such as the Brier score are more informative than AUC when comparing injury risk models.
paper.methods: Simulated 100 studies per condition at 1000 and 5000 observations, with ACWR values resampled from pooled Australian football and soccer data and injuries generated from U-shaped, flat or S-shaped risk profiles. Models were compared using RMSE against the true risk, false discovery and false rejection rates, and AUC, Brier and logarithmic scores estimated by 10-fold cross-validation. A longitudinal extension simulated correlated repeated observations (50 observations from 20 participants, or 100 from 50) and compared naive logistic regression with GEE.
paper.findings: Discrete models had higher RMSE than restricted cubic splines and fractional polynomials under the U-shaped and S-shaped profiles, and they fitted the true curve poorly. With a flat profile and 5000 observations, discrete models produced 16 to 21 false discoveries per 100 studies, against 7 for splines and 3 for fractional polynomials; false rejections at 1000 observations were high for quantile and cut-point models (59 and 57 of 100) but low for the z-score model (5 of 100). AUC selected a discrete model in 38 of 100 studies (U-shaped) and 31 of 100 (S-shaped), whereas Brier and logarithmic scores selected discrete models in 6 of 100 or fewer, and naive logistic regression missed the weakened longitudinal signal more often than GEE (47 vs 18 of 100).
paper.limitations: All injuries were simulated, and only a single covariate was modelled, so the multivariable and real-world behaviour of these methods was not tested. The risk profiles were assumed, and the U-shape was chosen to match the hypothesised relationship rather than estimated from injury data. The ACWR was calculated with one method (1-week acute, 4-week chronic, overlapping windows), and other calculation methods would change the value distribution.
paper.practicalImplications: When modelling training load against injury, avoid splitting continuous load into categories, and consider spline or fractional polynomial models. Judge candidate injury risk models with calibration measures such as the Brier or logarithmic score, not AUC alone. Where several observations come from the same athletes, account for the correlation (for example with GEE), since assuming independence inflated false rejections in the simulations.
paper.athleteDev: The paper does not test any training programme or performance outcome. Its use for staff is in how workload-injury models are built: keep load as a continuous variable rather than binning it, and do not treat a model's AUC as proof that one model is better for prescribing training.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return-to-sport decisions. The study used simulated injuries on squad training-load data and cannot set ACWR thresholds or return-to-play load limits for rehabilitating athletes.

records.sourceFile: More than a 2-fold risk of contralateral ACL injuries with ipsilateral graft failure 10 years after primary reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Grassi A, Macchiarola L, Lucidi GA, Stefanelli F, Neri M, Silvestri A, et al. More than a 2-fold risk of contralateral anterior cruciate ligament injuries compared with ipsilateral graft failure 10 years after primary reconstruction. Am J Sports Med. 2020;48(2):310-317.
paper.abstract: In 244 consecutive patients followed for a mean of 10 years after hamstring ACL reconstruction, contralateral ACL reconstruction was more common than ipsilateral revision (7.8% vs 3.4%). Patients younger than 18 years with a preoperative Tegner level of 7 or higher had the lowest survival (61.1% at 10 years for either knee).
paper.tldr: After hamstring ACL reconstruction, contralateral ACL reconstruction was more common than revision of the operated knee, with a significant difference from about year 6 onward. Young patients with a high preoperative activity level had the highest risk.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of a prospectively collected database from one centre, with all patients receiving the same single-bundle over-the-top reconstruction with lateral plasty using hamstring tendons. Follow-up was at a minimum of 10 years, with medical chart review and patient interview to identify further ACL surgery. Survival curves, log-rank tests, hazard ratios and stepwise logistic regression were used to test age, sex, BMI, smoking, preoperative Tegner level and timing of reconstruction.
paper.findings: Ipsilateral revision occurred in 8 patients (3.4%) and contralateral reconstruction in 19 (7.8%), and the 10-year survival free of a second ACL rupture was 89.3%. Patients younger than 18 (OR 4.0 for contralateral reconstruction) and those with preoperative Tegner level 7 or higher (OR 16.2) had higher risk, and the combination had 61.1% survival at 10 years. From year 6 onward, contralateral reconstruction was more likely than ipsilateral revision (hazard ratio 3.6 at 6 years, 95% CI 1.4 to 9.6, and 2.4 at 10 years, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.3).
paper.limitations: This was a retrospective single-centre series of one graft technique, and 15.1% of eligible patients were lost to follow-up. Injuries were identified by chart review and interview without objective examination, so subclinical failures may have been missed. Subgroup estimates are imprecise (for example the OR for Tegner level 7 or higher has a 95% CI of 2.1 to 124.0), and no return-to-sport data were collected.
paper.practicalImplications: Counsel patients that the uninjured knee may be at higher risk of ACL injury than the reconstructed knee in the years after surgery. Rehabilitation should address both knees, with particular attention to patients younger than 18 and those with high preoperative activity, as the authors recommend. The 40% figure for second injury in young, high-activity patients should be treated as a hypothesis to test, not a settled estimate.
paper.athleteDev: The paper has no performance outcomes. Its relevance for staff is injury prevention: the authors argue that the uninjured knee needs as much attention as the operated one in young athletes who take part in demanding sport.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return to sport because it argues for rehabilitating both knees, but the study did not record return to sport or any return-to-play test. It cannot be used to set clearance criteria or to judge readiness for sport.

records.sourceFile: Multiligament knee injury (MLKI) - An expert consensus statement on nomenclature, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation.pdf

paper.citation: Murray IR, Makaram NS, Geeslin AG, Chahla J, Moatshe G, Crossley K, et al. Multiligament knee injury (MLKI): an expert consensus statement on nomenclature, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2024.
paper.abstract: An international Delphi consensus of 39 experts agreed 50 statements on the nomenclature, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation of multiligament knee injury. The panel recommended a clear definition, a need for an updated classification, and individual decisions on surgery, with a multicentre registry and core outcome set as research priorities.
paper.tldr: An international expert panel reached agreement on 50 statements covering the definition, classification, imaging and treatment of multiligament knee injuries. It gives a clear definition and recommends MRI for suspected cases, but its timing and rehabilitation advice rests largely on expert opinion.
paper.methods: Modified Delphi consensus following British Journal of Sports Medicine guidelines and the ACCORD reporting checklist. Thirty-nine experts from 14 countries (31 men, 8 women), selected partly by publication count, completed three anonymous online rounds rating statements on a 5-point Likert scale; consensus required more than 75% agreement and fewer than 10% disagreement in the final round.
paper.findings: Experts agreed a definition of multiligament knee injury as a high-grade partial or complete tear of at least two major knee ligaments verified by examination or stress radiography (agreement 97.4%), and that most of these injuries are not caused by knee dislocation (agreement 79.5%). They recommended MRI for all suspected cases where available and a low threshold for CT angiography in high-energy injuries, and agreed single-stage surgery should be used whenever possible (agreement 80.6%) with decisions made on an individual basis. Early surgery was defined as within 21 days (agreement 76.3%), and a 4 to 6 week period of restricted weight-bearing was considered acceptable on low-order evidence (agreement 92.1%).
paper.limitations: The panel was weighted toward men, with 25 of 39 from North America and 28 orthopaedic surgeons, and expertise was judged by publication count, so the consensus may reflect that group; ethnicity and race were not collected. Many recommendations rest on expert opinion or low-order evidence, and rehabilitation timelines and content were not addressed. The abstract gives levels of agreement for operative management in young patients (100%) and single-stage surgery (92.3%) that differ from the agreement values in the tables (89.7% and 80.6%).
paper.practicalImplications: Medical and rehabilitation staff can adopt the consensus definition and classification principles when recording these injuries, and should avoid equating knee dislocation with multiligament injury unless a dislocation is confirmed. Surgical and staging decisions should be individual, based on injury pattern, associated injuries and patient factors, rather than on a fixed timeline.
paper.athleteDev: The statement does not address training load, performance or conditioning, so performance staff should use it only to inform communication with the medical team after a knee injury.
paper.rtp: The statement covers timing of surgery, single or staged surgery, and early range-of-motion work that bear on recovery time, but it sets no return-to-sport criteria, testing thresholds or timelines. Its weight-bearing period rests on low-order evidence and it does not address rehabilitation timelines, so return-to-play decisions still depend on the treating team's judgment.

records.sourceFile: Muscle architecture, morphology, and mechanical and functional properties of biceps femoris long head in professional soccer players with a prio.pdf

paper.citation: Nuñez FJ, Ritzmann R, Hernandez-Abad F, Martinez JC, Suarez-Arrones L. Muscle architecture, morphology, and mechanical and functional properties of biceps femoris long head in professional soccer players with a prior healed injured hamstring. J Clin Med. 2022;11:7222.
paper.abstract: Compared fascicle length, pennation angle, muscle thickness, stiffness and eccentric hamstring strength in 20 elite soccer players, 10 with a healed hamstring injury and 10 without. The injured limb had shorter biceps femoris long-head fascicles and higher proximal stiffness than the uninjured players' limbs. No significant differences were found between the injured and uninjured limbs of injured players, or in eccentric strength.
paper.tldr: In elite soccer players, a healed hamstring injury was associated with shorter biceps femoris long-head fascicles and stiffer proximal muscle, but the two limbs of injured players did not differ. Strength was not reduced, so this snapshot cannot show which players will re-injure.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional comparison of players from two squads, one in Switzerland and one in Italy. Fascicle length and pennation angle were measured with extended field-of-view B-mode ultrasound, stiffness with MyotonPRO, and eccentric strength by Nordic hamstring exercise on a NordBord and, in injured players only, by isokinetic dynamometry at 30 and 120 deg/s. Groups were compared with one-way ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.
paper.findings: The injured limb had a shorter BFlh fascicle (8.18 cm vs 9.41 and 9.46 cm in uninjured players' limbs; overall p = 0.039) and higher proximal stiffness (308 vs 269 and 260 N/m; overall p = 0.038). Injured and uninjured limbs of injured players did not differ on fascicle length, pennation angle, muscle thickness, stiffness or eccentric strength. NHE strength did not differ significantly between the injured limbs and the limbs of uninjured players. Isokinetic strength was measured only in injured players, so no between-group isokinetic comparison exists.
paper.limitations: The abstract describes muscle thickness as substantially lower in injured players, but Table 1 marks no significant difference for thickness (2.23 and 2.19 cm vs 2.42 and 2.39 cm). The Discussion says both legs of injured players had shorter fascicles and higher proximal stiffness, but only the injured-limb comparison is reported with a test. Sex is not reported, the sample is 20 players, the choice of players from the two squads is not explained, and only injured players completed the isokinetic test.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest that individual fascicle length and stiffness may be worth considering when designing prevention for players with a past hamstring injury. These data do not show that these measures predict re-injury, and no fascicle length threshold can be set from this study.
paper.athleteDev: Does not measure performance. Eccentric hamstring strength did not differ between groups, so the study gives no performance-based guidance.
paper.rtp: Can inform that players with a healed hamstring injury may show different muscle architecture and stiffness, but not that they are ready to return or at greater risk. It cannot be used as a return-to-play test, because the injured and uninjured limbs of injured players did not differ in fascicle length or strength.

records.sourceFile: Musculoskeletal Injury Risk After Sport-Related Concussion A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: McPherson AL, Nagai T, Webster KE, Hewett TE. Musculoskeletal injury risk after sport-related concussion: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Am J Sports Med. 2018.
paper.abstract: Ten studies of athletes with sport-related concussion and controls were reviewed, and eight were pooled with random-effects models. Athletes with concussion had 2.11 times the odds of a musculoskeletal injury after return to sport (95% CI 1.46 to 3.06) and a pooled incidence rate ratio of 1.67 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.96). The raised odds were seen in both male and female athletes.
paper.tldr: Athletes who had a concussion had about double the odds of a musculoskeletal injury after return to sport in pooled observational studies. The association held for both sexes, but the studies are small and mixed in design, and they cannot show that concussion causes the injuries.
paper.methods: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis following PRISMA. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched from January 2000 to November 2017 by two reviewers, with reference-list checks. Study quality was rated with the NIH tool for cohort and cross-sectional studies (6 to 11 of 14 items), and odds ratios and incidence rate ratios were pooled with the I2 index for heterogeneity.
paper.findings: Pooled odds ratio 2.11 (95% CI 1.46 to 3.06; I2 = 59%; 661 concussed and 1757 control athletes). Pooled incidence rate ratio 1.67 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.96; I2 = 0%). Sex-stratified odds ratios were 2.23 for female athletes (95% CI 1.40 to 3.57) and 2.06 for male athletes (95% CI 1.26 to 3.37), with no significant difference between the sexes (OR 1.53, 95% CI 0.86 to 2.70; p = 0.15).
paper.limitations: Included studies were mostly retrospective or prospective cohorts (level 3 evidence) with small samples, and control groups varied: matched non-concussed athletes in five studies, athletes with another injury in three, and none in one. Some studies reported athlete exposures poorly and had short follow-up, and two survey studies that could not establish the order of concussion and injury were excluded.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff managing return to sport after concussion should know that pooled odds of musculoskeletal injury after return were about twice those of controls in both male and female athletes, with no significant difference between the sexes. The authors recommend adding neuromuscular risk screening to return-to-sport protocols, but this review does not test whether such screening reduces injuries.
paper.athleteDev: Shows higher musculoskeletal injury rates after return from concussion, which bears on how closely staff monitor athletes once they are back in training. It does not measure performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: Can inform that athletes with a recent concussion had higher musculoskeletal injury rates after return, which is relevant to return-to-sport monitoring. It cannot set a return-to-play time, and it does not show that neuromuscular screening prevents injury.

records.sourceFile: NEXT-G~1.PDF

paper.citation: Juginović A, Kekić A, Aranza I, Biloš V, Armanda M. Next-Generation Approaches in Sports Medicine: The Role of Genetics, Omics, and Digital Health in Optimizing Athlete Performance and Longevity: A Narrative Review. Life. 2025;15:1023.
paper.abstract: Review of genetics, pharmacogenomics, digital health and multi-omics for precision sports medicine. Literature was searched in MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science and Cochrane Library for January 2018 to April 2024. The authors summarize gene variants linked to endurance, power, strength and injury, pharmacogenomic guidance for common sports medications, wearable and telemedicine tools, and multi-omics approaches, and propose a clinical framework.
paper.tldr: A review that proposes a staged framework for precision sports medicine: wearable monitoring through the season, genetic testing early in a career, pharmacogenomic testing before medication, and multi-omics profiling in the off-season. Most of the evidence is early-stage and qualitative, so the framework should be treated as a proposal rather than a validated protocol.
paper.methods: The authors call this a narrative review, but it describes a database search, so the library codes it as a systematic review by precedent. The Methods list MEDLINE (PubMed), EMBASE and Web of Science for January 2018 to April 2024 (the abstract also names Cochrane Library), using terms such as precision medicine, sports medicine, genomics and multi-omics, with forward and backward citation tracking. The synthesis was qualitative, with no screening counts or quality appraisal, and organized into four domains: genomics, pharmacogenomics, digital health and multi-omics.
paper.findings: The review links gene variants such as ACTN3, AMPD1, PPARGC1A and COL5A1 with performance or injury traits in the cited studies, and summarizes CPIC and DPWG dosing guidance for drugs metabolized by CYP2C9, CYP2D6 and CYP2C19. It reports that an acute-to-chronic workload ratio above 1.7 was associated with almost fivefold higher odds of contact injury in the cited work, and cites a study of eight NCAA Division I teams reporting a 60% injury decrease. Its multi-omics sections describe early associations rather than validated tools.
paper.limitations: The authors acknowledge possible bias in article selection and interpretation, and there is no quality appraisal or count of studies screened and included. The 60% injury-reduction claim is cited to a WHOOP press release (ref 102), not a peer-reviewed study. The authors also state that many genetic association studies are small and limited to specific populations, and the abstract names Cochrane Library while the Methods list only MEDLINE, EMBASE and Web of Science.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the framework as a discussion guide rather than a protocol. Before ordering genetic or pharmacogenomic tests for an athlete, confirm the specific gene-drug guideline and the governance and consent process for the test. Wearable load data can flag changes in training load, but the injury-reduction figure cited here comes from a commercial source and should not be assumed for a local program.
paper.athleteDev: The paper presents genetic profiling and multi-omics as early-stage ways to individualize training and nutrition, and treats wearable load metrics such as the acute-to-chronic workload ratio as useful for managing load. The genetic performance associations it cites are small, population-specific and not validated for selecting or programming individual athletes.
paper.rtp: The review suggests pharmacogenomic testing could make analgesic and other medication choices during recovery safer, and describes monitoring of recovery status. It gives no return-to-sport criteria or clearance tests, and its genetic injury-risk markers should not be used to decide return to play.

records.sourceFile: NON-CO~1.PDF

paper.citation: Chia L, De Oliveira Silva D, Whalan M, McKay MJ, Sullivan J, Fuller CW, et al. Non-contact Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Epidemiology in Team-Ball Sports: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis by Sex, Age, Sport, Participation Level, and Exposure Type. Sports Med. 2022.
paper.abstract: Systematic review with meta-analysis of 45 cohort studies of non-contact ACL injuries in team ball-sports, searched in six databases to July 2021. Non-contact injuries made up 55% of all ACL injuries (95% CI 48-62), and the overall incidence was 0.07 per 1000 player-hours (95% CI 0.05-0.10). Incidence was 0.14 per 1000 player-hours in females and 0.05 in males, and 0.48 during competition versus 0.04 during training, with high heterogeneity across studies.
paper.tldr: Across team ball-sports, non-contact ACL injuries account for a little over half of all ACL injuries, and most occur in competition rather than training. Female athletes had a significantly higher incidence per player-hour than males, but no significance test is reported for the sex difference in the proportion of non-contact injuries.
paper.methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020 and registered in PROSPERO (CRD42020179475). Six databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, CINAHL, Scopus, SPORTDiscus) were searched from inception to July 2021, and cohort studies reporting ACL injuries by mechanism were included. Pooled proportions and incidences used random-effects models, with meta-regression for sex, age group, sport, participation level and exposure type.
paper.findings: Forty-five studies reported 2,748 non-contact ACL injuries. The pooled proportion of non-contact to total ACL injuries was 55% (95% CI 48-62, I2 = 82%), with 63% in females and 50% in males, a difference the authors did not report as significant. Incidence per 1000 player-hours was 0.14 in females and 0.05 in males, a significant difference by meta-regression, and 0.48 in competition versus 0.04 in training, also significant. Incidence per 1000 player-hours was 0.06 in elite, 0.10 in intermediate and 0.13 in amateur athletes.
paper.limitations: Study quality was assessed with a modified six-item Newcastle-Ottawa scale, and authors of 22 of 46 included studies had to be contacted for non-contact data (the paper reports 45 included studies elsewhere). Heterogeneity was high, and many included studies defined non-contact mechanisms loosely, possibly including indirect contact. The abstract and conclusion state the proportion was higher in females without a reported significance test, and the participation-level results conflict by unit (amateur is higher per player-hour, intermediate higher per player-exposure). The amateur-level CI in Section 3.4.4 reads 45-767, which appears to be a typographical error.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the finding that most non-contact ACL injuries in these sports occur in competition as a prompt to review competition-specific risk factors, not as proof that training is safe. The sex difference in incidence per player-hour is a reason to examine female athletes' exposure and mechanisms, but staff should not assume the proportion of non-contact injuries differs by sex.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the review supports reporting injury data by mechanism, sex and exposure type so that ACL risk-reduction work targets the right settings. The participation-level and sport-level findings are inconclusive, so they should not be used to set training priorities for a specific squad.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport, rehabilitation or clearance decisions after ACL injury. Its incidence and proportion figures describe injury occurrence, so they should not be used to judge an individual athlete's readiness or re-injury risk.

records.sourceFile: Neurocognitive function and musculoskeletal injury risk in sports - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Wilke J, Groneberg D. Neurocognitive function and musculoskeletal injury risk in sports: a systematic review. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2021.
paper.abstract: A systematic review of the relationship between cognitive function and musculoskeletal injury in athletes. Nine cohort and case-control studies were included, most in college athletes in open-skill sports. Seven of nine studies suggested that lower-order cognitive function (visuomotor reaction time) was associated with injury, and none examined executive function.
paper.tldr: Nine studies suggest slower visuomotor reaction time may be linked to sport injury, mostly in college open-skill athletes. The evidence is limited and the authors call for prospective studies, including executive function, before any recommendations.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, with searches of PubMed, Web of Science and Google Scholar in March 2021 and reference-list checks. Two reviewers screened and rated studies with a modified Downs and Black checklist, giving a mean of 12 of 17 points.
paper.findings: Of nine eligible studies (seven cohort, two case-control), seven reported an association between lower-order cognition and injury, mainly slower reaction time. Examples include Dvorak et al. (injured soccer players with higher baseline reaction time than uninjured players, 128 ms and 134 ms vs 108 ms) and Wilkerson et al. (low performers with odds ratio 2.94 for lower extremity sprain or strain). Two studies (Faltus et al. in adolescent skiers and snowboarders, and Ha et al. in collegiate athletes) found no association.
paper.limitations: The authors note that the studies used different populations, outcomes and injury definitions, and most measured only lower-order functions. The text gives a reaction-time cut-off of 550 ms for one study, while the table gives 545 ms. Several included studies were retrospective, and one (Taimela et al.) gave no effect size.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest exercise professionals may consider developing screening measures addressing neurocognitive function, such as reaction time, as part of a multifactorial injury risk assessment. They state that several gaps must be addressed before definitive recommendations can be made, and that executive function needs further research.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff could consider reaction time as one measure in a broader assessment, but the review does not show that reaction time training improves performance. The authors note that intervention studies improved reaction time, and that it is unclear whether these gains translate into fewer injuries.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport. Its findings relate to injury risk in healthy athletes, not to decisions after an injury, so it should not be used for return-to-play clearance.

records.sourceFile: Neuromuscular Control Deficits and                                the Risk of Subsequent Injury after a     Concussion-   A         Scoping             Review.pdf

paper.citation: Howell DR, Lynall RC, Buckley TA, Herman DC. Neuromuscular Control Deficits and the Risk of Subsequent Injury after a Concussion: A Scoping Review. Sports Medicine. 2018.
paper.abstract: A scoping review of 32 studies in two linked areas: musculoskeletal injury risk after concussion (10 studies) and dual-task gait deficits after concussion (22 studies). The authors conclude that athletes appear more likely to sustain a musculoskeletal injury after concussion, and that dual-task neuromuscular deficits may persist after symptoms and clinical tests have recovered. The mechanism linking these findings is not yet tested.
paper.tldr: Athletes appear more likely to be injured after a concussion, and walking while performing a cognitive task can reveal deficits after symptoms and standard tests have recovered. The authors propose these deficits as one possible explanation, but it has not been tested directly.
paper.methods: Scoping review following PRISMA, with two searches of PubMed, Web of Science and Academic Search Premier from database inception to 9 December 2016, and reference-list checks. Two authors screened records independently and resolved discrepancies by consensus. No data quality assessment, effect size calculation or meta-analysis was performed.
paper.findings: Most of the 10 injury-risk studies reported a higher musculoskeletal injury risk after concussion, mainly for lower extremity injuries. For example, Brooks et al. reported odds of 2.48 and Herman et al. reported odds of 3.39 for lower extremity injury within 90 days in college athletes. The 22 dual-task gait studies generally reported altered gait under dual-task conditions for up to about two months after concussion, although some found no differences, for example in children.
paper.limitations: Results were not uniform: Nyberg et al. found no increased risk in professional ice hockey players compared with players with knee injuries, and some studies used injured comparison groups that could mask an effect. Injury definitions, follow-up periods and exposure differed across studies. The authors note that most dual-task gait studies came from a single laboratory, and that only one injury-risk study reported specifically on a female population (a sub-analysis of 25 cases).
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest that combined motor and cognitive tests may better reflect sport demands, and that including them in post-concussion examinations may help identify athletes at higher risk. Clinicians should treat this as a hypothesis, since the review does not show that these tests predict later injury.
paper.athleteDev: Performance and conditioning staff could consider cognitively loaded movement tasks when rebuilding athletes after concussion, since the authors argue these tasks resemble sport demands. The review reports no performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The review addresses return to play directly. It reports that some athletes show dual-task gait deficits at return to activity and that injury risk may be higher after return, but the authors describe the link as a hypothesis. It should not be used to set clearance criteria, because no study has shown that dual-task testing predicts injury after return.

records.sourceFile: New perspectives on risk factors for exterional heat stroke.pdf

paper.citation: Morrissey MC, Szymanski MR, Grundstein AJ, Casa DJ. New Perspectives on Risk Factors for Exertional Heat Stroke. Kinesiology Review. 2020;9(1):64-71.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of new perspectives on risk factors for exertional heat stroke (EHS), focusing on hydration, heat acclimatization, medical conditions, climate change and heat policies, medications, and strength and conditioning sessions. The authors state that EHS is survivable with appropriate care and that most cases should not occur in the first place.
paper.tldr: A narrative review of EHS risk factors. Heat acclimatization, fitness, hydration, weather-based activity modification and gradual return to training after inactivity are presented as the most practical controls. Several medication and supplement effects rest on small or animal studies.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy. It draws on the Rav-Acha et al. (2004) case series of more than 130 EHS cases, a 2019 meta-analysis of heat-mitigation strategies, data on NCAA and high school heat-acclimatization guidelines, and a Georgia high school football heat-policy study cited as in press.
paper.findings: The authors report that low fitness was present in 71% of the Rav-Acha cases and overweight in 64.7%. The 2019 meta-analysis ranked aerobic fitness as the most important protective factor, followed by heat acclimatization, pre-exercise cooling and hydration. After NCAA heat-acclimatization policies, EHS-related deaths fell by 95% from 2003 to 2016 (Adams et al., 2016). In the Georgia study, rates of heat syncope and heat exhaustion fell by 35% to 100% after the heat policy, depending on the WBGT category. The authors cite studies suggesting that each 1% of body-mass loss during exercise in the heat raises internal temperature by about 0.15 to 0.22 degrees C. In one cycling study, prescribed drinking gave a 5.1% (plus or minus 4.8%) speed advantage over ad libitum drinking (Bardis et al., 2017).
paper.limitations: This is a narrative review with no described search method, so study selection and the strength of each claim are not systematic. Much of the evidence comes from case series, observational studies, small trials and rodent work. The authors state that human NSAID evidence is limited and that the effects of creatine and caffeine are inconclusive. The Georgia policy study is cited before its publication.
paper.practicalImplications: Build fitness and heat acclimatization into preseason plans before athletes train in hot conditions, since the cited evidence links both to lower heat-illness risk. Use weather-based activity modification, and bring athletes back to training after inactivity in graded steps rather than at full workload. For hydration, start sessions euhydrated, and match the fluid strategy to the sport: programmed drinking where fluid cannot be taken during play, and drinking to thirst may suit cycling-type events.
paper.athleteDev: Use the review's points on fitness, heat acclimatization and gradual workload increases when planning training-camp and preseason heat exposure. The review states that untrained athletes are more susceptible to heat illness, so new or returning athletes need graded loading. Stimulant medications and dehydrating medications should be reviewed before hot-weather training.
paper.rtp: The review addresses EHS prevention and does not give return-to-play criteria for an athlete who has had a heat stroke. Its guidance on returning to training after a break is about prevention, and it notes that prevention strategies differ from the treatment of EHS. It cannot be used to clear an athlete after EHS.

records.sourceFile: No Clinical Predictors of Postconcussion Musculoskeletal Injury in College Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Buckley TA, Howard CM, Oldham JR, Lynall RC, Swanik CB, Getchell N. No Clinical Predictors of Postconcussion Musculoskeletal Injury in College Athletes. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2020;52(6):1256-1262.
paper.abstract: In 66 NCAA athletes with concussion and a matched subset of 36 non-concussed teammates, concussed athletes had a higher hazard of lower-extremity musculoskeletal injury in the year after return to play (HR 1.78, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.84). Demographic, injury and acute concussion assessment measures did not predict which concussed athletes were later injured.
paper.tldr: Athletes who had a concussion were about 1.8 times as likely to sustain a lower-extremity musculoskeletal injury in the following year as matched teammates. Standard concussion measures and demographics did not identify which concussed athletes were at risk, so they cannot yet be used to target prevention.
paper.methods: Cohort study of 66 intercollegiate athletes with a diagnosed concussion who completed a baseline and an acute (within 48 hours) battery: symptom checklists, SAC, BESS, ImPACT, clinical reaction time and the King-Devick test. Change scores (acute minus baseline) and demographic and injury variables were entered into two logistic regression models for subsequent lower-extremity MSK injury. A matched subset of 36 concussed athletes was compared with 36 non-concussed teammates, with time to injury analysed by Cox proportional hazards over one year before and after return to play.
paper.findings: Concussed athletes had a hazard ratio of 1.78 for subsequent lower-extremity MSK injury compared with matched controls (95% CI 1.12 to 2.84; P = .015), with no difference in the year before concussion. Among athletes who were injured, mean time to injury was 160 days in the concussion group and 244 days in controls (P < .001). Neither the demographic and injury model (P = .318) nor the clinical concussion model (P = .461) predicted subsequent injury, and no individual predictor was significant.
paper.limitations: The matched subset is small (36 concussed athletes and 36 controls), and the authors state that the study was underpowered to identify individual predictors. The sample followed CARE protocols with a mean time loss of 18.4 days, which the authors note is well beyond the commonly reported 7 to 10 days, and included one university's NCAA athletes only. The year-before comparison is reported inconsistently: Results give a between-group HR of 0.858 (95% CI 0.52 to 2.09, P = .910), but the Discussion cites P = .795, Exp(B) = 0.858, which are the Table 4 logistic-regression values for prior injury (95% CI 0.270 to 2.723) within concussed athletes only; the Results CI is also not centred on 0.858, so one of these figures is likely a reporting error.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat the year after return from concussion as a period of raised lower-extremity injury risk: in this matched cohort the hazard was 1.78 times that of teammate controls. Standard concussion measures, demographics and injury presentation did not identify who was at risk, so they should not be used alone to select athletes for prevention work. The authors recommend considering injury prevention strategies at return to play, but this study did not test any intervention.
paper.athleteDev: Lower-extremity injury risk was higher in the year after concussion in this cohort, and injuries came sooner (mean 160 vs 244 days). The study did not test monitoring, load management or any prevention program, and it does not identify which athletes are at greatest risk, so it cannot guide individual training decisions.
paper.rtp: This study is directly relevant to return to play after concussion. Athletes in the cohort had returned to baseline and completed a progressive protocol, and the concussed group still had a higher lower-extremity injury risk over the following year. It does not test whether any concussion measure can clear an athlete to return, and it cannot be used to judge readiness to return.
